plain_english: In the morning when you don't want to get up, think about this right away: I'm being called to do human work. Am I really unwilling to do what I was born for? What I was brought into this world to do? Was I made to lie around and pamper myself in a warm bed? 'But this feels good.' Is that what you were born for — to enjoy pleasure? Weren't you made to always be busy and working? Look at everything else in the world. Every tree and plant. Sparrows and ants. Spiders and bees. All of them focus on doing their part to keep this orderly universe going. Won't you do what belongs to humans? Won't you rush to do what your nature requires?
original_excerpt: In the morning when thou findest thyself unwilling to rise, consider with thyself presently, it is to go about a man's work that I am stirred up. Am I then yet unwilling to go about that, for which I myself was born and brought forth into this world? Or was I made for this, to lay me down, and make much of myself in a warm bed? 'O but this is pleasing.' And was it then for this that thou wert born, that thou mightest enjoy pleasure? Was it not in very truth for this, that thou mightest always be busy and in action? Seest thou not how all things in the world besides, how every tree md plant, how sparrows and ants, spiders and bees: how all in their kind are intent as it were orderly to perform whatsoever (towards the preservation of this orderly universe) naturally doth become and belong unto thin? And wilt not thou do that, which belongs unto a man to do? Wilt not thou run to do that, which thy nature doth require?

plain_english: 'But you need rest.' Yes, you do. Nature allows you a certain amount of rest, just like eating and drinking. But you go beyond what you need. You exceed what would be enough. Yet when it comes to action, you fall short of what you could do. This means you don't love yourself. If you did, you would also love your nature and what your nature aims for. Look at others who enjoy their work. They can wear themselves out at their jobs. They neglect their bodies and food for it. Do you honor your nature less than a common worker honors his trade? Less than a good dancer honors his art? Less than a greedy man loves his money, or a vain man loves applause? When these people care about something, they're willing to go without food and sleep to pursue it. So why do actions that serve the common good of humanity seem worse to you? Why do they deserve less respect and effort?
original_excerpt: 'But thou must have some rest.' Yes, thou must. Nature hath of that also, as well as of eating and drinking, allowed thee a certain stint. But thou guest beyond thy stint, and beyond that which would suffice, and in matter of action, there thou comest short of that which thou mayest. It must needs be therefore, that thou dost not love thyself, for if thou didst, thou wouldst also love thy nature, and that which thy nature doth propose unto herself as her end. Others, as many as take pleasure in their trade and profession, can even pine themselves at their works, and neglect their bodies and their food for it; and doest thou less honour thy nature, than an ordinary mechanic his trade; or a good dancer his art? than a covetous man his silver, and vainglorious man applause? These to whatsoever they take an affection, can be content to want their meat and sleep, to further that every one which he affects: and shall actions tending to the common good of human society, seem more vile unto thee, or worthy of less respect and intention?

plain_english: How easy it is to push away all those chaotic, outside thoughts and be at perfect peace right away!
original_excerpt: How easy a thing is it for a man to put off from him all turbulent adventitious imaginations, and presently to be in perfect rest and tranquillity!

plain_english: Think of yourself as capable of speaking or doing what feels natural and right. Don't let criticism or gossip stop you. If something is right and honest to say or do, don't sell yourself short by backing down. Other people have their own minds and their own ways of thinking. Don't waste time watching what they do. Just keep moving forward where your own nature and the common good both point you. The path is the same for both.
original_excerpt: Think thyself fit and worthy to speak, or to do anything that is according to nature, and let not the reproach, or report of some that may ensue upon it, ever deter thee. If it be right and honest to be spoken or done, undervalue not thyself so much, as to be discouraged from it. As for them, they have their own rational over-ruling part, and their own proper inclination: which thou must not stand and look about to take notice of, but go on straight, whither both thine own particular, and the common nature do lead thee; and the way of both these, is but one.

plain_english: I keep living according to nature until I fall and stop, breathing my last breath into the same air I breathed all my life. I will fall on the same earth that gave the materials for my father's seed, my mother's blood, and my nurse's milk. This earth fed and watered me for years. It carries me as I walk on it. It puts up with me even though I abuse it and use it freely in so many ways for so many purposes.
original_excerpt: I continue my course by actions according to nature, until I fall and cease, breathing out my last breath into that air, by which continually breathed in I did live; and falling upon that earth, out of whose gifts and fruits my father gathered his seed, my mother her blood, and my nurse her milk, out of which for so many years I have been provided, both of meat and drink. And lastly, which beareth me that tread upon it, and beareth with me that so many ways do abuse it, or so freely make use of it, so many ways to so many ends.

plain_english: No one can admire you for sharp, clever speech — you just don't have that gift. Fine. But there are many other good things you can't blame on lack of natural ability. Show the qualities that depend entirely on you: honesty, seriousness, hard work, contempt for pleasures. Don't complain. Be content with little. Be kind. Be generous. Avoid excess and empty chatter. Be noble in spirit. Don't you see how many things you could do and show, despite any excuse about natural weakness? Yet you still choose to stay down in the dumps.
original_excerpt: No man can admire thee for thy sharp acute language, such is thy natural disability that way. Be it so: yet there be many other good things, for the want of which thou canst not plead the want or natural ability. Let them be seen in thee, which depend wholly from thee; sincerity, gravity, laboriousness, contempt of pleasures; be not querulous, be Content with little, be kind, be free; avoid all superfluity, all vain prattling; be magnanimous. Doest not thou perceive, how many things there be, which notwithstanding any pretence of natural indisposition and unfitness, thou mightest have performed and exhibited, and yet still thou doest voluntarily continue drooping downwards?

plain_english: Or will you say it's your natural makeup that forces you to complain, to be low and miserable, to flatter people? That makes you blame others one moment and try to please them the next? That drives you to chase praise, to be scattered and restless in your thoughts? No — the gods know better. You could have been free of all this long ago. The only thing you'd have to accept is being called a bit slow or dull. And even with that, you could train yourself not to worry about this weakness or take pride in it.
original_excerpt: Or wilt thou say that it is through defect of thy natural constitution, that thou art constrained to murmur, to be base and wretched to flatter; now to accuse, and now to please, and pacify thy body: to be vainglorious, to be so giddy-headed., and unsettled in thy thoughts? nay (witnesses be the Gods) of all these thou mightest have been rid long ago: only, this thou must have been contented with, to have borne the blame of one that is somewhat slow and dull, wherein thou must so exercise thyself, as one who neither doth much take to heart this his natural defect, nor yet pleaseth himself in it.

plain_english: Some people do a good deed and then expect payment for it. They want something back. Others don't demand payment, but they still think the person owes them something. They keep track of what they've done. But there are others who do good things and don't even think about it afterward. They're like a vine that grows grapes. Once it has produced its fruit, it's satisfied and doesn't look for any reward. After a horse runs a race, or a hunting dog finishes the hunt, or a bee makes honey, they don't wait around for praise. The same goes for someone who truly understands their nature. When they do something good, they just move on to the next good thing. Like the vine that bears fruit in season and then gets ready to bear fruit again.
original_excerpt: Such there be, who when they have done a good turn to any, are ready to set them on the score for it, and to require retaliation. Others there be, who though they stand not upon retaliation, to require any, yet they think with themselves nevertheless, that such a one is their debtor, and they know as their word is what they have done. Others again there be, who when they have done any such thing, do not so much as know what they have done; but are like unto the vine, which beareth her grapes, and when once she hath borne her own proper fruit, is contented and seeks for no further recompense. As a horse after a race, and a hunting dog when he hath hunted, and a bee when she hath made her honey, look not for applause and commendation; so neither doth that man that rightly doth understand his own nature when he hath done a good turn: but from one doth proceed to do another, even as the vine after she hath once borne fruit in her own proper season, is ready for another time.

plain_english: So you must be one of those people who just do things without thinking much about it. They hardly notice what they're doing. 'But wait,' someone might say, 'a thinking person should understand what he's doing. That's what makes us naturally social — we're aware that we're helping others, and we want them to notice it too.' What you're saying sounds right, but you don't really understand what it means. So you're actually one of those first people I mentioned. They also think they have good reasons. But if you want to truly understand what this means, don't worry — you won't stop doing good things for others.
original_excerpt: Thou therefore must be one of them, who what they do, barely do it without any further thought, and are in a manner insensible of what they do. 'Nay but,' will some reply perchance, 'this very thing a rational man is bound unto, to understand what it is, that he doeth.' For it is the property, say they, of one that is naturally sociable, to be sensible, that he doth operate sociably: nay, and to desire, that the party him self that is sociably dealt with, should be sensible of it too. I answer, That which thou sayest is true indeed, but the true meaning of that which is said, thou dost not understand. And therefore art thou one of those first, whom I mentioned. For they also are led by a probable appearance of reason. But if thou dost desire to understand truly what it is that is said, fear not that thou shalt therefore give over any sociable action.

plain_english: The Athenians used to pray like this: 'O rain, rain, good Jupiter, on all the lands and fields that belong to the Athenians.' Either we should not pray at all, or we should pray this way — completely and freely, not just for ourselves alone.
original_excerpt: The form of the Athenians' prayer did run thus: 'O rain, rain, good Jupiter, upon all the grounds and fields that belong to the Athenians.' Either we should not pray at all, or thus absolutely and freely; and not every one for himself in particular alone.

plain_english: We say the doctor has prescribed one man riding, another cold baths, and a third walking barefoot. In the same way, the nature of the universe has prescribed sickness, blindness, loss, or damage to different people. When we say a doctor prescribed something, we mean he assigned it to help with healing. So whatever happens to anyone was meant for them by fate. This is why we say things "fall together." When square stones fit perfectly in walls or pyramids, masons say they "fall together" in harmony. Even though the individual things are different, they create one unified pattern.
original_excerpt: As we say commonly, The physician hath prescribed unto this man, riding; unto another, cold baths; unto a third, to go barefoot: so it is alike to say, The nature of the universe hath prescribed unto this man sickness, or blindness, or some loss, or damage or some such thing. For as there, when we say of a physician, that he hath prescribed anything, our meaning is, that he hath appointed this for that, as subordinate and conducing to health: so here, whatsoever doth happen unto any, is ordained unto him as a thing subordinate unto the fates, and therefore do we say of such things, that they do συμβαίνειν, that is, happen, or fall together; as of square stones, when either in walls, or pyramids in a certain position they fit one another, and agree as it were in an harmony, the masons say, that they do συμβαίνειν; as if thou shouldest say, fall together: so that in the general, though the things be divers that make it, yet the consent or harmony itself is but one.

plain_english: The whole world is made up of all the individual bodies in it — one complete body that works the same way as individual bodies do. In the same way, the destiny of individual causes and events is part of one general destiny that works like individual causes do. Even simple people understand this. They say 'This is what fate brought him' — meaning his destiny brought this to him specifically. So fate brings each thing to each person in particular, just like a doctor prescribes specific treatments for specific patients. We should accept what fate brings us the same way we accept what doctors prescribe. Medicine often tastes bitter and harsh, but we take it anyway because we hope it will make us healthy.
original_excerpt: And as the whole world is made up of all the particular bodies of the world, one perfect and complete body, of the same nature that particular bodies; so is the destiny of particular causes and events one general one, of the same nature that particular causes are. What I now say, even they that are mere idiots are not ignorant of: for they say commonly τοῦτο ἔφερεν ἀυτῷ, that is, This his destiny hath brought upon him. This therefore is by the fates properly and particularly brought upon this, as that unto this in particular is by the physician prescribed. These therefore let us accept of in like manner, as we do those that are prescribed unto us our physicians. For them also in themselves shall We find to contain many harsh things, but we nevertheless, in hope of health, and recovery, accept of them.

plain_english: Let the things that nature has set in motion be like your own health to you. Accept whatever happens, even when it feels harsh and unpleasant. See it as serving a purpose—the health of the universe and the good of all things. Whatever happens to you would not have occurred unless it helped the whole universe. No force in nature creates anything that doesn't serve its proper role. For these two reasons, you should be content with whatever happens to you.
original_excerpt: Let the fulfilling and accomplishment of those things which the common nature hath determined, be unto thee as thy health. Accept then, and be pleased with whatsoever doth happen, though otherwise harsh and un-pleasing, as tending to that end, to the health and welfare of the universe, and to Jove's happiness and prosperity. For this whatsoever it be, should not have been produced, had it not conduced to the good of the universe. For neither doth any ordinary particular nature bring anything to pass, that is not to whatsoever is within the sphere of its own proper administration and government agreeable and subordinate. For these two considerations then thou must be well pleased with anything that doth happen unto thee.

plain_english: First, what happened to you was meant for you specifically. It was assigned to you from the very beginning through the chain of causes that led to this moment. Second, the success and health of the whole universe—and even its continued existence—depends on each part playing its role. The whole is complete and perfect only when all its parts stay connected. If you cut away any piece, you damage the links between parts and causes. And you do cut something away—as much as you can—whenever you resist what happens to you.
original_excerpt: First, because that for thee properly it was brought to pass, and unto thee it was prescribed; and that from the very beginning by the series and connection of the first causes, it hath ever had a reference unto thee. And secondly, because the good success and perfect welfare, and indeed the very continuance of Him, that is the Administrator of the whole, doth in a manner depend on it. For the whole (because whole, therefore entire and perfect) is maimed, and mutilated, if thou shalt cut off anything at all, whereby the coherence, and contiguity as of parts, so of causes, is maintained and preserved. Of which certain it is, that thou doest (as much as lieth in thee) cut off, and in some sort violently take somewhat away, as often as thou art displeased with anything that happeneth.

plain_english: Don't get frustrated. Don't get discouraged. Don't lose hope. Often you won't do everything perfectly according to what is right. When you fall short, just come back to it again. You will face many distractions from the world and human weaknesses. As a person, you can't avoid these completely. Don't be upset about them. But love and care for the one thing you can return to: living like a philosopher and doing your work in the most careful way. When you come back to philosophy, don't approach it like some students do — returning to their teachers after time off, as if it were a chore. Instead, be like someone with sore eyes reaching for a sponge and egg white. Or like someone reaching for a healing bandage. Or like others reaching for warm compresses. Don't make following reason into a show. Make it your comfort and relief.
original_excerpt: Be not discontented, be not disheartened, be not out of hope, if often it succeed not so well with thee punctually and precisely to do all things according to the right dogmata, but being once cast off, return unto them again: and as for those many and more frequent occurrences, either of worldly distractions, or human infirmities, which as a man thou canst not but in some measure be subject unto, be not thou discontented with them; but however, love and affect that only which thou dust return unto: a philosopher's life, and proper occupation after the most exact manner. And when thou dust return to thy philosophy, return not unto it as the manner of some is, after play and liberty as it were, to their schoolmasters and pedagogues; but as they that have sore eyes to their sponge and egg: or as another to his cataplasm; or as others to their fomentations: so shalt not thou make it a matter of ostentation at all to obey reason but of ease and comfort.

plain_english: Remember that philosophy asks nothing of you except what your nature already asks. Would you really want anything that goes against nature? Which do you think is more pleasant and agreeable — what follows nature or what fights against it? Isn't this why pleasure itself brings so many people to ruin? Because it seems natural and pleasant? But think about this: aren't true greatness, real freedom, honesty, balance, and goodness more natural and pleasant? And wisdom itself — what could be more agreeable when you consider what it means to move through life using your mind properly, without stumbling?
original_excerpt: And remember that philosophy requireth nothing of thee, but what thy nature requireth, and wouldest thou thyself desire anything that is not according to nature? for which of these sayest thou; that which is according to nature or against it, is of itself more kind and pleasing? Is it not for that respect especially, that pleasure itself is to so many men's hurt and overthrow, most prevalent, because esteemed commonly most kind, and natural? But consider well whether magnanimity rather, and true liberty, and true simplicity, and equanimity, and holiness; whether these be not most kind and natural? And prudency itself, what more kind and amiable than it, when thou shalt truly consider with thyself, what it is through all the proper objects of thy rational intellectual faculty currently to go on without any fall or stumble?

plain_english: The true nature of worldly things is so wrapped in mystery that many great philosophers found them completely beyond understanding. Even the Stoics, who think we can grasp them, say it's barely possible and very difficult. So all our judgments are shaky — who among us never makes mistakes? Now move from thinking about the nature of things to their actual substance. How temporary and worthless they are! They might belong to some disgusting person, some prostitute, or some well-known tyrant who steals from others.
original_excerpt: As for the things of the world, their true nature is in a manner so involved with obscurity, that unto many philosophers, and those no mean ones, they seemed altogether incomprehensible, and the Stoics themselves, though they judge them not altogether incomprehensible, yet scarce and not without much difficulty, comprehensible, so that all assent of ours is fallible, for who is he that is infallible in his conclusions? From the nature of things, pass now unto their subjects and matter: how temporary, how vile are they I such as may be in the power and possession of some abominable loose liver, of some common strumpet, of some notorious oppressor and extortioner.

plain_english: Think about the people you spend time with every day. How hard it is to put up with them, even the ones we love most! I won't even mention how hard it is to put up with ourselves. Everything is so unclear and messy. Everything keeps changing — the world itself, time, movement, the things that move. What can we hold onto? What deserves our respect or our serious effort? I can't even imagine. These things seem to work against each other.
original_excerpt: Pass from thence to the dispositions of them that thou doest ordinarily converse with, how hardly do we bear, even with the most loving and amiable! that I may not say, how hard it is for us to bear even with our own selves, in such obscurity, and impurity of things: in such and so continual a flux both of the substances and time; both of the motions themselves, and things moved; what it is that we can fasten upon; either to honour, and respect especially; or seriously, and studiously to seek after; I cannot so much as conceive For indeed they are things contrary.

plain_english: You must find comfort in knowing that your natural death will come, and meanwhile not worry about the delay. Rest easy in two truths. First, nothing will happen to you that goes against the nature of the universe. Second, you have the power to do nothing against your own inner god and spirit. No one can force you to betray what is sacred within you.
original_excerpt: Thou must comfort thyself in the expectation of thy natural dissolution, and in the meantime not grieve at the delay; but rest contented in those two things. First, that nothing shall happen unto thee, which is not according to the nature of the universe. Secondly, that it is in thy power, to do nothing against thine own proper God, and inward spirit. For it is not in any man's power to constrain thee to transgress against him.

plain_english: What am I doing with my soul right now? You must ask yourself this question often, at every moment: what is my mind focused on? Whose soul do I have? A child's? A young person's? A woman's? A tyrant's? Some animal's? Some wild beast's?
original_excerpt: What is the use that now at this present I make of my soul? Thus from time to time and upon all occasions thou must put this question to thyself; what is now that part of mine which they call the rational mistress part, employed about? Whose soul do I now properly possess? a child's? or a youth's? a woman's? or a tyrant's? some brute, or some wild beast's soul?

plain_english: You can see what things truly are by looking at what most people call "good." When someone hears about real goods — wisdom, self-control, justice, courage — and really understands them, they can't bear to hear anything else called "good." The word belongs to these things alone.
original_excerpt: What those things are in themselves, which by the greatest part are esteemed good, thou mayest gather even from this. For if a man shall hear things mentioned as good, which are really good indeed, such as are prudence, temperance, justice, fortitude, after so much heard and conceived, he cannot endure to hear of any more, for the word good is properly spoken of them.

plain_english: But when ordinary people hear things called 'good' that they think are good, they want to hear more. A person is happy to hear what comedians say on stage as just everyday talk that regular people understand. Why else would it be fine when comedians call virtues good without any excuse needed? But when they praise wealth, pleasure, or honor, we only take it as a joke? Keep thinking about this. Ask yourself if the things that get mocked on stage — where the crowd laughs at rich people who own so much they don't even have a private place to relieve themselves — ask if those things should really be valued as truly good.
original_excerpt: But as for those which by the vulgar are esteemed good, if he shall hear them mentioned as good, he doth hearken for more. He is well contented to hear, that what is spoken by the comedian, is but familiarly and popularly spoken, so that even the vulgar apprehend the difference. For why is it else, that this offends not and needs not to be excused, when virtues are styled good: but that which is spoken in commendation of wealth, pleasure, or honour, we entertain it only as merrily and pleasantly spoken? Proceed therefore, and inquire further, whether it may not be that those things also which being mentioned upon the stage were merrily, and with great applause of the multitude, scoffed at with this jest, that they that possessed them had not in all the world of their own, (such was their affluence and plenty) so much as a place where to avoid their excrements. Whether, I say, those ought not also in very deed to be much respected, and esteemed of, as the only things that are truly good.

plain_english: Everything I'm made of is either form or matter. Nothing can destroy either of these completely — I didn't come from nothing to begin with. Every part of me will change and become part of the world. Then it will change again into something else, and so on forever. This same endless change made me what I am now. It made my parents what they were, and their parents before them, going back forever. We can think this way even though the world itself might run in cycles with clear beginnings and ends.
original_excerpt: All that I consist of, is either form or matter. No corruption can reduce either of these unto nothing: for neither did I of nothing become a subsistent creature. Every part of mine then will by mutation be disposed into a certain part of the whole world, and that in time into another part; and so _in infinitum;_ by which kind of mutation, I also became what I am, and so did they that begot me, and they before them, and so upwards _in infinitum_. For so we may be allowed to speak, though the age and government of the world, be to some certain periods of time limited, and confined.

plain_english: Reason works by itself and is satisfied with its own proper actions. It starts moving on its own. But it moves straight toward whatever goal lies in front of it — whatever is actually possible to achieve. This might be different from what it first set out to do. That's why these actions are called "right actions" — because they follow the straight path to what can actually be done. Nothing belongs to a person unless it belongs to them as a human being. The outcomes of our plans are not what we require as humans. Human nature doesn't promise such things. The final results of our actions have nothing to do with our nature as people. So a person's purpose — the highest good that fulfills that purpose — cannot depend on completing the plans we set out to achieve.
original_excerpt: Reason, and rational power, are faculties which content themselves with themselves, and their own proper operations. And as for their first inclination and motion, that they take from themselves. But their progress is right to the end and object, which is in their way, as it were, and lieth just before them: that is, which is feasible and possible, whether it be that which at the first they proposed to themselves, or no. For which reason also such actions are termed κατορθώσεις, to intimate the directness of the way, by which they are achieved. Nothing must be thought to belong to a man, which doth not belong unto him as he is a man. These, the event of purposes, are not things required in a man. The nature of man doth not profess any such things. The final ends and consummations of actions are nothing at all to a man's nature. The end therefore of a man, or the _summum bonum_ whereby that end is fulfilled, cannot consist in the consummation of actions purposed and intended.

plain_english: Think about these outside things — money, status, possessions. If they truly belonged to human nature, then it would be wrong to reject them or oppose them. A person who could live without them wouldn't be praised for it. And if these things were actually good, then someone who gave them up willingly wouldn't be called virtuous. But we see the opposite is true. The more someone pulls away from external wealth and status, or handles losing these things well, the more we respect them.
original_excerpt: Again, concerning these outward worldly things, were it so that any of them did properly belong unto man, then would it not belong unto man, to condemn them and to stand in opposition with them. Neither would he be praiseworthy that can live without them; or he good, (if these were good indeed) who of his own accord doth deprive himself of any of them. But we see contrariwise, that the more a man doth withdraw himself from these wherein external pomp and greatness doth consist, or any other like these; or the better he doth bear with the loss of these, the better he is accounted.

plain_english: Whatever you think about regularly is what your mind becomes. The soul gets its color from your thoughts and imagination. So dye it completely with constant good thoughts. For example: wherever you live, you have the power to live well and be happy. You might live at court — well then, you can live well and be happy there too.
original_excerpt: Such as thy thoughts and ordinary cogitations are, such will thy mind be in time. For the soul doth as it were receive its tincture from the fancies, and imaginations. Dye it therefore and thoroughly soak it with the assiduity of these cogitations. As for example. Wheresoever thou mayest live, there it is in thy power to live well and happy. But thou mayest live at the Court, there then also mayest thou live well and happy.

plain_english: Everything is made for a purpose, and naturally moves toward that purpose. Where something finds its purpose, there it finds its good. So society is the natural good for rational beings like us. We have long known that we are made for community. Can anyone doubt that lower things serve higher things? That the best things are made to work together? That things with souls are better than things without souls? And that among those with souls, the ones with rational souls are best?
original_excerpt: Again, that which everything is made for, he is also made unto that, and cannot but naturally incline unto it. That which anything doth naturally incline unto, therein is his end. Wherein the end of everything doth consist, therein also doth his good and benefit consist. Society therefore is the proper good of a rational creature. For that we are made for society, it hath long since been demonstrated. Or can any man make any question of this, that whatsoever is naturally worse and inferior, is ordinarily subordinated to that which is better? and that those things that are best, are made one for another? And those things that have souls, are better than those that have none? and of those that have, those best that have rational souls?

plain_english: To want impossible things is madness. But it's impossible for wicked people not to do wicked things. Nothing happens to you that doesn't naturally happen to people like you. The same things happen to others too. If someone who doesn't understand what happened to them can stay calm, or if someone seeking praise for being brave can bear it without complaint — isn't it sad that ignorance or vanity should be stronger than real wisdom?
original_excerpt: To desire things impossible is the part of a mad man. But it is a thing impossible, that wicked man should not commit some such things. Neither doth anything happen to any man, which in the ordinary course of nature as natural unto him doth not happen. Again, the same things happen unto others also. And truly, if either he that is ignorant that such a thing hath happened unto him, or he that is ambitious to be commended for his magnanimity, can be patient, and is not grieved: is it not a grievous thing, that either ignorance, or a vain desire to please and to be commended, should be more powerful and effectual than true prudence?

plain_english: Things themselves cannot touch the soul. They have no way to reach it or affect it. The soul can only be moved by itself. Whatever beliefs and opinions the soul accepts — that's what shapes how it experiences the things around it.
original_excerpt: As for the things themselves, they touch not the soul, neither can they have any access unto it: neither can they of themselves any ways either affect it, or move it. For she herself alone can affect and move herself, and according as the dogmata and opinions are, which she doth vouchsafe herself; so are those things which, as accessories, have any co-existence with her.

plain_english: In one sense, other people are closest to us. We should help them and put up with them. But when someone gets in the way of what I need to do, that person becomes just another obstacle to me — like the sun, wind, or a wild animal. Some of these things might block what I'm trying to do. But they can't touch my mind or my will. My mind has a built-in ability to step back and shift focus — from what can't be done to what can be done. The mind turns any obstacle into its main target. What was blocking the way becomes the way forward.
original_excerpt: After one consideration, man is nearest unto us; as we are bound to do them good, and to bear with them. But as he may oppose any of our true proper actions, so man is unto me but as a thing indifferent: even as the sun, or the wind, or some wild beast. By some of these it may be, that some operation or other of mine, may be hindered; however, of my mind and resolution itself, there can be no let or impediment, by reason of that ordinary constant both exception (or reservation wherewith it inclineth) and ready conversion of objects; from that which may not be, to that which may be, which in the prosecution of its inclinations, as occasion serves, it doth observe. For by these the mind doth turn and convert any impediment whatsoever, to be her aim and purpose. So that what before was the impediment, is now the principal object of her working; and that which before was in her way, is now her readiest way.

plain_english: Honor what is most important and powerful in the world — the thing that uses all things and governs all things. Do the same in yourself. Honor what is most important and powerful in you. It is the same kind of thing we just talked about. This same force in you turns everything else to its own use. It governs your life too.
original_excerpt: Honour that which is chiefest and most powerful in the world, and that is it, which makes use of all things, and governs all things. So also in thyself; honour that which is chiefest, and most powerful; and is of one kind and nature with that which we now spake of. For it is the very same, which being in thee, turneth all other things to its own use, and by whom also thy life is governed.

plain_english: What doesn't hurt the city itself can't hurt any citizen. Remember this rule whenever you think someone has wronged you. If the whole city isn't harmed by this, then neither am I. And if the whole isn't harmed, why should I take it personally? Instead, think about where the person who seems to have wronged you went astray.
original_excerpt: That which doth not hurt the city itself; cannot hurt any citizen. This rule thou must remember to apply and make use of upon every conceit and apprehension of wrong. If the whole city be not hurt by this, neither am I certainly. And if the whole be not, why should I make it my private grievance? consider rather what it is wherein he is overseen that is thought to have done the wrong.

plain_english:
Think often about how quickly everything in the world gets swept away and disappears. The things themselves flow like a river. All actions are constantly changing. Even the causes behind things shift in a thousand ways. Almost nothing stays the same.

Next, consider the endless time that came before you and the vast time that will come after, when everything will dissolve and disappear. Aren't you foolish, then, to get puffed up with pride over these things? Or to worry yourself sick? Or to complain as if something could really trouble you for very long?
original_excerpt: Again, often meditate how swiftly all things that subsist, and all things that are done in the world, are carried away, and as it were conveyed out of sight: for both the substance themselves, we see as a flood, are in a continual flux; and all actions in a perpetual change; and the causes themselves, subject to a thousand alterations, neither is there anything almost, that may ever be said to be now settled and constant. Next unto this, and which follows upon it, consider both the infiniteness of the time already past, and the immense vastness of that which is to come, wherein all things are to be resolved and annihilated. Art not thou then a very fool, who for these things, art either puffed up with pride, or distracted with cares, or canst find in thy heart to make such moans as for a thing that would trouble thee for a very long time?

plain_english: Think about the whole universe — you are just a tiny part of it. Think about all of time — you get only a short moment. Think about all the events that happen — how little of it actually touches you! Now, someone wrongs me. That's his problem. He controls his own mind and actions. I am busy with what nature gives me to have. And what my own nature tells me to do, I do.
original_excerpt: Consider the whole universe whereof thou art but a very little part, and the whole age of the world together, whereof but a short and very momentary portion is allotted unto thee, and all the fates and destinies together, of which how much is it that comes to thy part and share! Again: another doth trespass against me. Let him look to that. He is master of his own disposition, and of his own operation. I for my part am in the meantime in possession of as much, as the common nature would have me to possess: and that which mine own nature would have me do, I do.

plain_english: Don't let the ruling part of your mind be controlled by physical pain or pleasure. Keep it separate from these feelings. Let those feelings stay in the body where they belong. But sometimes in our connected body and mind, physical sensations will affect your thoughts. That's natural. When this happens, don't try to fight the feeling itself. Just don't let your mind add judgments about whether the sensation is good or bad. The pain or pleasure in your flesh means nothing to who you really are. If you can avoid judging it, you'll be fine.
original_excerpt: Let not that chief commanding part of thy soul be ever subject to any variation through any corporal either pain or pleasure, neither suffer it to be mixed with these, but let it both circumscribe itself, and confine those affections to their own proper parts and members. But if at any time they do reflect and rebound upon the mind and understanding (as in an united and compacted body it must needs;) then must thou not go about to resist sense and feeling, it being natural. However let not thy understanding to this natural sense and feeling, which whether unto our flesh pleasant or painful, is unto us nothing properly, add an opinion of either good or bad and all is well.

plain_english: To live with the Gods. A person lives with the Gods when they always show them a soul that is content and pleased with whatever happens to them. They do whatever pleases that divine spirit — part of themselves — that Zeus has given to each person as their guide and ruler.
original_excerpt: To live with the Gods. He liveth with the Gods, who at all times affords unto them the spectacle of a soul, both contented and well pleased with whatsoever is afforded, or allotted unto her; and performing whatsoever is pleasing to that Spirit, whom (being part of himself) Jove hath appointed to every man as his overseer and governor.

plain_english: Don't get angry with someone whose breath smells bad, or whose armpits stink. What can he do about it? That's just how his breath is naturally, and that's how his armpits are. From those things, that smell has to come. 'But,' you say, 'the man has a brain and could figure out that standing close to people will offend them.' Well, you have a brain too. Use your reason to work on his reason. Show him the problem. Give him advice. If he listens to you, you've helped him, and you won't need to be angry anymore.
original_excerpt: Be not angry neither with him whose breath, neither with him whose arm holes, are offensive. What can he do? such is his breath naturally, and such are his arm holes; and from such, such an effect, and such a smell must of necessity proceed. 'O, but the man (sayest thou) hath understanding in him, and might of himself know, that he by standing near, cannot choose but offend.' And thou also (God bless thee!) hast understanding. Let thy reasonable faculty, work upon his reasonable faculty; show him his fault, admonish him. If he hearken unto thee, thou hast cured him, and there will be no more occasion of anger.

plain_english: You might dream of a place 'where there are no troublemakers or corrupt people.' Why dream of that? You plan to live virtuously when you retire to some perfect place where bad people don't exist. You can do the same thing right here. And if people won't let you live well, you can leave life itself rather than abandon your principles. But leave like someone who doesn't feel wronged. Just like someone saying, 'There's smoke here; I'll go outside.' What's the big deal? Until something forces me out, I'll stay free. No one will stop me from doing what I choose. And what I choose will always be guided by my nature as a thinking, social being.
original_excerpt: 'Where there shall neither roarer be, nor harlot.' Why so? As thou dost purpose to live, when thou hast retired thyself to some such place, where neither roarer nor harlot is: so mayest thou here. And if they will not suffer thee, then mayest thou leave thy life rather than thy calling, but so as one that doth not think himself anyways wronged. Only as one would say, Here is a smoke; I will out of it. And what a great matter is this! Now till some such thing force me out, I will continue free; neither shall any man hinder me to do what I will, and my will shall ever be by the proper nature of a reasonable and sociable creature, regulated and directed.

plain_english: The rational force that governs the universe is built for community and connection. It has made the worse things serve the best. It has bound the best things together in harmony. Can't you see how it has arranged everything in order? How it has given each thing what it deserves? And the highest things of all — it has united them in agreement.
original_excerpt: That rational essence by which the universe is governed, is for community and society; and therefore hath it both made the things that are worse, for the best, and hath allied and knit together those which are best, as it were in an harmony. Seest thou not how it hath sub-ordinated, and co-ordinated? and how it hath distributed unto everything according to its worth? and those which have the pre-eminency and superiority above all, hath it united together, into a mutual consent and agreement.

plain_english: How have you treated the gods so far? Your parents? Your brothers and sisters? Your wife? Your children? Your teachers? Those who raised you? Your friends? Your household? Your servants? Can you honestly say that you have never wronged any of them with your words or actions?
original_excerpt: How hast thou carried thyself hitherto towards the Gods? towards thy parents? towards thy brethren? towards thy wife? towards thy children? towards thy masters? thy foster-fathers? thy friends? thy domestics? thy servants? Is it so with thee, that hitherto thou hast neither by word or deed wronged any of them?

plain_english: Remember all the things you have already been through and endured. Your life story is already full. Your duty is complete. Think of all the truly good things you have recognized. How many pleasures and pains have you looked past with indifference? How many supposedly glorious things have you seen through? How kindly and wisely have you treated difficult, unreasonable people?
original_excerpt: Remember withal through how many things thou hast already passed, and how many thou hast been able to endure; so that now the legend of thy life is full, and thy charge is accomplished. Again, how many truly good things have certainly by thee been discerned? how many pleasures, how many pains hast thou passed over with contempt? how many things eternally glorious hast thou despised? towards how many perverse unreasonable men hast thou carried thyself kindly, and discreetly?

plain_english: Why should foolish, ignorant souls disturb what is both wise and learned? And what is this wise thing? It is the soul that understands the beginning and the end. It truly knows that rational essence that flows through all existing things and through all time, staying always the same. It arranges and governs the universe in cycles.
original_excerpt: Why should imprudent unlearned souls trouble that which is both learned, and prudent? And which is that that is so? she that understandeth the beginning and the end, and hath the true knowledge of that rational essence, that passeth through all things subsisting, and through all ages being ever the same, disposing and dispensing as it were this universe by certain periods of time.

plain_english: Very soon you will be either ashes or bones. Maybe you'll leave behind a name. Maybe not even that. And what is a name anyway? Just an empty sound that echoes and fades. The things we care about most in life — the things we think matter — are actually worthless, rotten, and pathetic. Even the most serious and important matters, if you really look at them, are like puppies fighting each other. Or like bratty children laughing one minute and crying the next.
original_excerpt: Within a very little while, thou wilt be either ashes, or a sceletum; and a name perchance; and perchance, not so much as a name. And what is that but an empty sound, and a rebounding echo? Those things which in this life are dearest unto us, and of most account, they are in themselves but vain, putrid, contemptible. The most weighty and serious, if rightly esteemed, but as puppies, biting one another: or untoward children, now laughing and then crying.

plain_english: Faith, modesty, justice, and truth have long since left this wide earth and gone to heaven, as one poet put it. So what keeps you here? Physical things change and shift constantly. Your senses are dim and unreliable. Your soul is just vapor from blood. Being respected by such people is empty. What are you waiting for? Death or transformation — either way, face it calmly. But until that time comes, what will satisfy you? Nothing except worshipping the gods and doing good for others. Put up with people. Don't harm them. Remember that everything outside you — your weak body, your life itself — none of it belongs to you or is under your control.
original_excerpt: As for faith, and modesty, and justice, and truth, they long since, as one of the poets hath it, have abandoned this spacious earth, and retired themselves unto heaven. What is it then that doth keep thee here, if things sensible be so mutable and unsettled? and the senses so obscure, and so fallible? and our souls nothing but an exhalation of blood? and to be in credit among such, be but vanity? What is it that thou dost stay for? an extinction, or a translation; either of them with a propitious and contented mind. But still that time come, what will content thee? what else, but to worship and praise the Gods; and to do good unto men. To bear with them, and to forbear to do them any wrong. And for all external things belonging either to this thy wretched body, or life, to remember that they are neither thine, nor in thy power.

plain_english: You can always make progress if you choose the right path. In both your thoughts and actions, follow a true method. Two things are common to all souls — God's, human, and every thinking being. First, nothing can stop them from doing their proper work. Second, their happiness comes from wanting to do what is right and actually doing it. This is where their desire ends.
original_excerpt: Thou mayest always speed, if thou wilt but make choice of the right way; if in the course both of thine opinions and actions, thou wilt observe a true method. These two things be common to the souls, as of God, so of men, and of every reasonable creature, first that in their own proper work they cannot be hindered by anything: and secondly, that their happiness doth consist in a disposition to, and in the practice of righteousness; and that in these their desire is terminated.

plain_english: If this is not my wrongdoing, and does not come from any fault of mine, and the public is not harmed — why should it concern me? How could the public be hurt? Don't let yourself be swept away by assumptions and popular opinion. You should help others as best you can when the situation calls for it, even if they suffer losses in worldly matters. But don't imagine they are truly damaged by these things. That would be wrong.
original_excerpt: If this neither be my wicked act, nor an act anyways depending from any wickedness of mine, and that by it the public is not hurt; what doth it concern me? And wherein can the public be hurt? For thou must not altogether be carried by conceit and common opinion: as for help thou must afford that unto them after thy best ability, and as occasion shall require, though they sustain damage, but in these middle or worldly things; but however do not thou conceive that they are truly hurt thereby: for that is not right.

plain_english: Think of the old foster-father in the play. When he's leaving, he carefully asks for his foster-child's toy rattle back — but he remembers it's just a toy. Do the same thing here. What is all this arguing and shouting in the courts really about? Have you forgotten what these things actually are? Yes, but other people care deeply about them and think they're important. Will you be a fool too? I was once. Let that be enough.
original_excerpt: But as that old foster-father in the comedy, being now to take his leave doth with a great deal of ceremony, require his foster-child's rhombus, or rattle-top, remembering nevertheless that it is but a rhombus; so here also do thou likewise. For indeed what is all this pleading and public bawling for at the courts? O man, hast thou forgotten what those things are! yea but they are things that others much care for, and highly esteem of. Wilt thou therefore be a fool too? Once I was; let that suffice.

plain_english:
Let death surprise me when it will, and where it will. I can still be a happy man.

A happy man is one who gives himself a happy lot in life. A happy lot means good inclinations of the soul, good desires, and good actions.
original_excerpt:
Let death surprise me when it will, and where it will, I may be εὔμοιρος, or a happy man, nevertheless.

For he is a happy man, who in his lifetime dealeth unto himself a happy lot and portion. A happy lot and portion is, good inclinations of the soul, good desires, good actions.
